title: Making Retrieval Practice Actually Work: Seven Essential Principles for Teachers to Know
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick argues that despite retrieval practice being one of the most robustly evidence-based learning strategies available, many schools are implementing it poorly -- mandating it at the start of every lesson without understanding the underlying mechanisms that make it work. He lays out seven principles: forgetting is a necessary precondition for effortful, memory-strengthening retrieval; retrieval should function as a learning event, not just an assessment event; initial retrieval needs enough challenge to avoid the 'illusion of competence'; retrieval must be spaced over time rather than crammed; it should be meaningfully connected to the curriculum rather than randomly generated; students need to be explicitly taught retrieval strategies like elaboration and generative retrieval; and it should stay low-stakes to avoid triggering anxiety that undermines the very process it's meant to support. Hendrick draws a key distinction between retrieval strength (how easily information can be accessed right now) and storage strength (how durably it's consolidated), arguing that effortful retrieval after some forgetting builds both. He closes by flagging future posts on how spacing and interleaving work synergistically with retrieval practice in real classrooms.
points: Hendrick's central diagnostic: retrieval practice used purely for assessment (mark right/wrong, move on) forfeits its main benefit, which comes from the effortful reconstruction process itself, not from measuring what's already known.

The 'illusion of competence' warning -- easy, too-soon retrieval feels like mastery but produces fragile, context-dependent memories -- explains why quizzing immediately after teaching often backfires.

Retrieval divorced from curriculum sequencing (his jab at 'random kahoots off the internet') weakens both motivation and encoding, because students perceive unlinked recall tasks as busywork rather than meaningful practice.

Retrieval is presented as a teachable skill, not an innate one -- students need explicit instruction in strategies like elaboration and generative question-writing to get full benefit from retrieval practice.
quotes: Retrieval practice, the act of actively recalling information from memory rather than simply re-reading or reviewing it, is one of the most powerful evidence-based learning strategies we have.
As Robert Bjork explains, the very act of forgetting creates the conditions necessary for stronger relearning, making temporary forgetting a feature, not a bug, of how our memory systems work.
When retrieval practice is used solely for assessment purposes, it can create anxiety and pressure, which can be detrimental to learning, especially if it's high-stakes.
Giving quizzes, where the first retrieval is very soon after learning, can create the "illusion of competence" where students recall easily on that first attempt, but later performance suffers.
Recognising that a problem us a quadratic equation is not the same as being able to solve it.
Randomly asking students to recall facts without any context or purpose is unlikely to be effective. (Stop getting random kahoots off the internet).

Retrieval practice is most effective when it's low-stakes and stress-free. High-stakes tests, while sometimes necessary, can trigger anxiety that interferes with retrieval and reduces the learning benefits.
